record.tranche_reason: The study probes for information remaining after training a behavior away, using a synthetic trigger rather than a standard unlearning benchmark or attack.
record.gate_note: The trigger behavior was deliberately trained into the model; its initial expression is not evidence of naturally occurring behavior. The post-training probes directly measure whether trigger information remains detectable. The cited 38% result from Patil et al. and the WMDP Figure 9 result are not this study's results. A comment mentions refusal-related probes only qualitatively and without reported numerical results.
record.test_reason: In a new setting, a deliberately trained trigger behaviour is removed by normal-only LoRA fine-tuning. Linear probes then check whether trigger information persists internally. This is analogous to version C's claim that the method blocks access rather than deleting. It is not a standard knowledge-unlearning method, and no recovery attack is run.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The author concludes that fine-tuning the behaviour away does not undo trigger training, and that internals persist longer than behaviour. Probe accuracy nonetheless drops below 100%, and the author calls the experiment weakly designed and hard to interpret.
record.recipe_differences: The study deliberately trains a synthetic conditional trigger behavior, then LoRA-fine-tunes on normal completions regardless of the trigger. It does not apply a standard knowledge-unlearning method or test a recovery attack.
record.method_sensitivity: The best probing layer shifted: layer 16 gave the highest accuracy in the round-2 runs, while layer 13 was about 5% more accurate at the end of extended training. Later token positions caused small quantitative changes.

fits_no_version.finding: Training the decision-tree trigger in raised probe accuracy from 74% (untrained) to 100% from layer 13 onward.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training a conditional trigger makes that trigger linearly decodable from mid-layer activations.

fits_no_version.finding: About 200 normal-only examples removed the trained 'urpr' trigger behaviour essentially completely (plotted; no numbers in the text).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normal-only fine-tuning suppresses a trained backdoor behaviour quickly.

fits_no_version.finding: In a comment, the author reports that probes for a median-task answer were similar whether or not the model refused (qualitative, no numbers).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Models compute the answer internally even when refusing.

record.peer_reviewed: LessWrong post; peer review not stated
record.problems: The authors call the experiment weak and difficult to interpret. It uses one comparatively small model and LoRA rather than full fine-tuning; the trigger is an intentionally trained conditional policy rather than undesired generalization; the probe baseline is already non-trivial; plotted behavior frequencies are not stated numerically; and no uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: No numerical refusal-probe results are given in the comment, so they are not recorded. Cited results from Patil et al. and WMDP are excluded because they are not this study's own results.

untested.parts: No activation-direction ablation and no behavioural recovery of the suppressed behaviour. No standard unlearning method (e.g. RMU, gradient ascent) and no factual or hazardous knowledge target.
Not tested: no near-chance knowledge accuracy, no general-ability check, no simple attacks.

missing.what: Accuracy of probes trained on the initial (pre-removal) model's activations and applied during normal-only training (blue curve), plus the green 'urpr' frequency values. Both are plotted only.
Layer-16 probe accuracy at the end of extended training (implied ~80%, about 5% below layer 13).
missing.locator: What if one trains much longer?

record.verdict_notes: This is borderline as a test of C: the target is a deliberately trained conditional behaviour, not knowledge, and the removal method is plain fine-tuning rather than an unlearning method. The cited 38% figure from Patil et al. and the WMDP Figure 9 result are not this study's results. The baseline is messy because features such as gender correlate with the trigger, which the author acknowledges. The record's 'supports' label and its two-label split for the same condition are merged into one limits_scope label, and r2 is removed from the label because it is not linked to C.

versions.untested_parts: Does not assess targeted-knowledge accuracy near chance, retained general ability, or whether simple attacks fail.
Does not test recovery through fine-tuning on a small relearning set after forgetting.
No activation-direction ablation or behavioral recovery attack; the study probes trigger information after training the trigger behavior away.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, language variation, or in-context recovery test.
No newer counter-method or robustness evaluation.
